title: “And When Will the DEA Investigate the Narcos and Laundering in the U.S.?” Sheinbaum Asks
author: Denisse Torres Hernández
content:
_This article by[Denisse Torres
Hernández](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/denissetorres/) originally
appeared in the [November 26, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4910408/y-la-dea-cuando-investigara-a-
los-narcos-y-el-lavado-en-eu-cuestiona-la-presidenta/), an independent Mexican
digital news outlet._

_Sheinbaum defended Mexico 's results against organized crime and asked what
the U.S. government is doing to stop the distribution of drugs and money
laundering on its own territory._

**Mexico City, November 26 (SinEmbargo).-** President **Claudia Sheinbaum
Pardo** (**CSP**) criticized on Thursday that the **U.S. Drug Enforcement
Administration** (**DEA**) is enabling telephone lines to receive **reports**
from **Mexico** about alleged links of officials and associates with the
[**Sinaloa Cartel**](https://www.sinembargo.mx/tag/cartel-de-sinaloa/), while
the agency has pending investigations into **drug trafficking** ,
**corruption** and **money laundering** in its own country.

The federal government's **Security Cabinet** joined her questioning,
rejecting any unilateral action by the [U.S.
agency](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4909353/la-dea-dejo-pasar-1-4-millones-de-
pastillas-de-fentanilo-para-investigar-narcos-ap/) and warning that the
country does not accept interference in its territory.

During her morning press conference, the federal head of state considered that
this initiative represents interference in Mexican affairs and raised what
would happen if the federal government did the same to receive information
about alleged acts of corruption on U.S. territory.

> Imagine if the Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection opened a
> WhatsApp for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the United
> States government see it?
>
> President Claudia Sheinbaum

For that reason, she insisted that U.S. authorities should concentrate on
investigating what happens within their own borders, instead of enabling
mechanisms to receive reports on matters that correspond to Mexican
institutions.

"It is evident that it is a matter of interference because… Let's put up the
news story. The DEA has a lot to do in its own country, a lot. The first thing
it should be doing is investigating corruption in the United States linked to
organized crime, or what they call 'terrorist groups,'" she stated.

## Security Cabinet Rejects Unilateral Actions by the DEA

In a message on its social media, the Security Cabinet reiterated that Mexico
"has institutions empowered to receive complaints, investigate crimes, combat
corruption and prevent impunity."

> Following the DEA's announcement, it maintained that "each country must
> assume the responsibilities that correspond to it in the fight against
> organized crime."

> Ante el anuncio de la @DEAHQ, el Gabinete de Seguridad del @GobiernoMX
> reitera que México no acepta acciones unilaterales ni injerencias en su
> territorio.
>
> [Post by @GabSeguridadMX on
> X](https://twitter.com/GabSeguridadMX/status/2125989602276040870)

The Mexican government also reaffirmed its willingness to maintain
international cooperation, although it established four principles for that
relationship.

"We reaffirm our commitment to international cooperation, always under four
inalienable principles: full respect for sovereignty and territorial
integrity, shared and differentiated responsibility, mutual respect and trust,
and **cooperation without subordination** ," it insisted.

## What Is the DEA Doing Against Fentanyl Trafficking in the U.S.?

As part of her arguments, President Sheinbaum Pardo cited an investigation by
the _Associated Press_ (AP) news agency about an operation in which the DEA
allowed thousands of fentanyl pills to circulate during an investigation in
the U.S.

In her response, she compared that case with the operation known as "Fast and
Furious," through which weapons were allowed to enter and circulate into
Mexico, and questioned the actions of U.S. authorities in the face of drug
trafficking: "Recently a news story came out. Look at how serious this is.
It's from AP, a recognized news agency. 'The DEA let thousands of fentanyl
pills circulate in a major probe.' This is one of many cases, **a fentanyl
'Fast and Furious,' only in the United States**. Where is the DEA's action?"

![Sheinbaum shows an AP report on a DEA
investigation](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/02-dea-
ap-fentanyl.jpg)Sheinbaum showed an AP publication about a DEA investigation
related to the circulation of fentanyl on U.S. territory. Photo: Presidencia

Sheinbaum also put the U.S. drug market on the table and asked who is in
charge of distributing the narcotics, as well as where the profits from their
illegal sale end up, particularly fentanyl.

"As we have said many times, what, there's no drug trafficking in the United
States? Well, that's where the consumption is. Who distributes the drugs?
**Where does the money from the distribution and sale of illegal fentanyl in
the United States end up?** " she questioned.

In contrast, she defended her government's actions against criminal
organizations, including the dismantling of methamphetamine labs, the seizure
of fentanyl pills and the arrests of members of criminal groups. She also
highlighted that these operations have involved risks for soldiers, members of
the National Guard and agents of the Secretariat of Security and Citizen
Protection.

The federal head of state stated that homicides in Mexico have fallen
practically 50 percent, recalled the sending of 94 criminals to the United
States, and maintained that her administration works daily to reduce violence
and help stop drug trafficking into that country.

> “One Pill Can Kill,” the DEA warned the public for years. Yet agents let at
> least 1.4 million fentanyl pills go unseized as they spent months monitoring
> a trafficking ring across six states, an AP investigation found.
>
> [Post by @APjoshgoodman on
> X](https://twitter.com/APjoshgoodman/status/2125230485127524553)

Finally, she insisted that bilateral cooperation must include actions on both
sides of the border and not be limited to U.S. authorities receiving
information about what happens in Mexico.

> "Our relevant and reciprocal question is what is the United States doing in
> the United States, because now it turns out that it has a phone line so that
> Mexicans can report to the DEA in the United States something that happens
> in Mexico. Here there is an Attorney General's Office, here the Secretariat
> of Security works. So they should pay a lot of attention on the other side
> of the border."
